blocks.x: So it's going. My name is Alton Ponyo. I was born 726 St. Peter Street, right down in old Korea.
Right there.
I was born April 16, 1911. I'm 47 right now. I didn't hear much music around that time.
Did your parents play any music?
My daddy played a little drums, but not with any bands to mount anything. And of course my mother was just a housewife.
How many brothers and sisters? A little bit about your family?

I have one brother who is now a saxophone player. His name is Théodore Ponyo. I think he's been a little sick. But the last report I got from him that he was coming along real nicely. And I said we lived around this neighborhood until I imagine around 9, 10 years of age. And then my mother moved out of the old career. We moved into, which was more of a colored section. And that's where I began to pick up on his jazz music.
What was the first music you remember hearing when you were a kid? Parades? The parades?

No, it wasn't the parades. It was these advertisements that the bands on the truck, the tailgate music, was the first music that I heard, this jazz music like that. And we used to sit on the corner, they had bread boxes, the groceries. The bread man used to leave the bread in the box in the morning. And we used to take sticks and beat on the bread boxes because it sounds something like a drum.
How much then, your brother is older than you? Yeah, my brother is three years older than I am. My brother should be 50 now. So, oh man. Okay. So you started out as a drummer.
Yeah, I first wanted to play drums, you know. But, I don't know, I never did get around to it that much. So, finally my mother, later on my mother moved right next door to the old cooperators hall.
Oh yeah. That's the same way they call Hope's Hall. Yeah.
And that's where I heard all these great jazz bands like Chris Kelly, Guy Kelly, Papa Celestan, Kid Renee, and Manuel Perez.
Buddy Petit.
Buddy Petit. Yeah, I heard all that. I heard, when I was small also, I heard Louis Armstrong's but it was in Perez.
Yeah.
I got a many whippers at night when they'd have these balls at the cooperators hall, you know. At that time, nine o'clock children had to be in bed.
Yeah.

And I'd sneak out and try to listen up to the band. My mother would miss me and fan me good. Yeah. But that's where I really began to love that music. But it wasn't then that I got the idea of playing music.
Well that cooperators is a church now, right? Yeah. Did you hear any good church music when you were a kid? Oh yeah. Did you belong to any church?

Yeah, I was christened Catholic but my mother was Baptist and we used to go to a church that's not far from the cooperators hall, it was on Liberty and St. Peter. And it was, the pastor's name was Ella Cole.
It's still there. I think you're going to tear that place down now. It's still there? I think maybe there's one out there on St. Peter.

St. Peter and Liberty, yeah. The auditorium. That's right. And at that time, we used to call it Ella Cole's Church. And oh, they had some wonderful singing. I heard preachers like Blind Frank, which was one of the greatest preachers they had in New Orleans as I knew of at that time. But I used to have all these choirs, I used to love that. I used to love to go to church and hear this singing. I didn't know much about the church but I loved the singing, you know? But what really inspired me to play music, I was, I went to school and in school I mean, I used to sing. And I had a pretty good voice, you know? And later years I had a lot of piano players like Lil Willie, Georgie, Parker, Red Caillou and all those fellas. And I used to sing with them at house parties. And then I met this little guy who became a wonderful friend of mine, this little boy in San Diego, who was a marvelous piano player. And I began to go around with him singing at different parties and different things, bumming around with him. So I used to like to sing so much that he showed me some chords on the piano. He wasn't a reader but he could play a lot of piano. What type of piano did he play?
He wasn't just a blues man. He played any type of piano.

He played classic, regs, popular, anything he heard he played and he played it very well. Anybody in New Orleans will tell you that. That's right. He was one of the greatest piano players. He began to show me a few little chords on the piano and then when I wasn't with him I'd go around some balls that had a piano in practice. Well I learned how to play Stagger Lee and different other blues you know that they played down there. And I met a fellow one time at a ballroom who taught me how to play Indian Love Call. That was the first popular number I learned how to play. And I learned how to play it in C, which is written in E flat. But I always not, still play it in C when I play. And that started me, fooling around with the piano.
Was your brother already playing something that?

Yeah. My brother at that time had begun to take up the saxophone and we were living together. And oh they used to have ten and fifteen fellas every day used to rehearse them back there. They rehearsed them so much that I knew a number from the introduction to the corner stop. I could whistle it, I mean without making a mistake. But anyhow he became a very wonderful musician and I'm very proud of him. He was one of the top saxophone players down in New Orleans, which I think he still is if he can still play. But me I wanted to battle house, you know, and he wanted me to take music. In fact one time he tried to learn me how to play the saxophone. And man I'm telling you we laughed so much I never could get nothing. He would kid me and I would laugh and he would laugh and I just quit. But the first job I ever got was with, I was standing on the corner and things was tough during the depression. And some people came down looking for a piano player. Well I couldn't play over two pieces but I could sing a lot you know. And they were looking for this piano player George E. Parker. And they asked me did I know where he was. So I told them well I knew a couple of places that he might be. So I got in the car with them and went looking for him and we never could find him. So one of the fellas mentioned said we just could find a fella who could play one or two pieces. So I told them I could play one or two pieces. So they said well that's good enough. And we went well around the lake which I was lost when I got out there. And I really did a good job. The singing really put me over you know. That was your first job.
My first job. You got paid for it.

Yeah wait the trouble was when I knocked off the man asked me how much did he owe me. And I didn't know what to charge him. And I needed money so badly. But I said ten dollars you know. And which was very high at that time. You just wasn't getting that kind of money. But I didn't know what to charge so I said ten dollars. You know I wanted to be a big shot. So the man gave me fifteen dollars anyhow. And I was rich man. Yeah that was good.
Well I bet you wanted to be a musician at that time. Yeah.

Then I began to play a little cheap jobs for a dollar and a half. And what you could drink was just fun to me. The money didn't mean anything. I mean we just loved to play you know. And I'd get a drum and piano and my singing helped me out a whole lot. So I still was bumming with this little guy at Boynton San Diego. And he was a fellow, he didn't like to play for money. He liked to play for pleasure. And he had a little job at the Pelican N.A.s. And he quit the job. And I had sit in with them a couple of times. And they had a banjo player. We used to call him Van. His name is Joe. And he begged me to take the job. He said I could play enough and he would help me. So he persuaded me and I took the job. I was so nervous. But every day he would show me how to build certain cards and different things like that. And I was so much interested and I called on right away. And I had the pleasure of playing on this job. The steamer, all the fellows off the steamer capital used to come and jam. And I would just sit down and call. I couldn't play that much. I just could call. And I would call maybe one number for our. We had all the greatest musicians in the South playing down there. Sun Johnson and Taft off the boat and Eugene Porter and oh just a lot of great musicians that now have made a big name for themselves. And I stood on this job for oh maybe a year or something. And after I got off that job I think I knew every chord that they were playing at that time. So I got interested in it. My brother thought that I was interested in it. Then he began to explain to me a little about music. At this time my brother was playing with Walter Pichon's band. And I became good friends with Walter and Walter used to teach me.
Was he working on the boat those days or right at the top?

That was before he worked on the boat. And of course right after that they got a job on the boat. And well I learned a little bit about music. It's enough to take a piece in practice and play you know. Which made me get along pretty well. And then Sam Morgan died and his brother Isaiah kind of took over a band and made the trips that he used to make. He used to play all over the south.
You get your coke and stuff and drink. You have to keep talking. That's right.
And so they hired me with the band and gave me a tryout. Well I was pretty good on my chords. Isaiah was very strict. He wanted a rhythm section to play rhythm.
He's back in town now. He's back in town now? Yeah.

Well I worked with Isaiah oh two, three years. And I never would come home with any money. We used to play percentage jobs. When we were on a trip some of the jobs were percentage. Some of them were paid jobs and different things. But as far as I got the money I wanted to have plenty for it and I'd spend it. But anyhow I got a lot of band experience with Isaiah. And then after I left Isaiah's band I began to get a little trios. And my singing helped me out most because I never could play too much solo work. And I used to sing. I played, I remember playing a job before Bourbon Street was Bourbon Street. They had two places on Bourbon Street. Bourbon Street was a residential. They didn't have anything around Bourbon. And until Sturryville was completely closed because after it was supposed to be closed the people were over there illegal you know. And I worked on Bourbon with this Albert Walkers, they called Albert Fernandez. We had Lionel Turrigano who also played drum with, a young guy like me played drum with Isaiah Morgan too. He was my friend. And we worked the thrill there. Which we worked for about three or four years. And after I left that job, then I used to work jobs with George Lewis. Used to play different jobs. I remember one time that I got a job for some girls to dance. It was during the war. And we went around the army camp and it was a drummer by the name of Robert Davis and myself and I had George Lewis to play with us. And we stood on that job about two or three weeks. But then things was too bad over there for me. So we came on back home. And then I got jobs playing singles. And then I was playing in the evening at the house that Jack built which was on Bourbon. Bourbon was building up now. And right on the corner the famous door opened up and Smiley and Joe had the band and their piano player left. And I went and worked with Smiley and Joe. And I was working day and night. I had this day job working playing cocktail hours and that night. I worked that for about two months but man that was too hard. So I continued playing with Smiley and Joe and then I would, when George Lewis would get jobs or something like that they would hire me. I played several jobs with Keith Howard. And by this time I was getting pretty good on chords and one of the things I had to do in these little country towns playing with bands, the pianos were so bad that a piano player had the cross chord. And I was interested in it and it was very easy for me to cross chord. Sometimes I was playing in F sharp and B natural, things like that, which very few piano players
could do. You were playing with a different key than the rest of the band. That's right, with the rest of the band. You could raise up the pitch.

You could raise up the band. You could raise up the band. So I quit working on Bourbon Street and I went back to town and hanging around a while. And Sidney Desvind, who had one of the best bands in New Orleans, their piano player wanted to go on a vacation. Who was it, remember? William Huston, who was also the president of the music union then. And they had a lot of good piano players around there that was much better than me, such as Kato. In fact I met him in San Diego about five months ago. I played up there. What's his name again? Kato. Adam Kato. No, it was Kates.
No, no, Kates.

No, this guy was named K-A-T-O, Kato. Well anyhow, Sidney hired a couple of these real good piano players and Sidney was very strict. You had to play his music as is, you know. You don't put no rest. They wanted to be hot, so he had to fire them. I don't know how he'd become the high of me, but anyhow, I wasn't that good a musician. At that time Alvin Alcorn was playing with the band and my brother was playing with the band.
All real top musicians, you know.
I was really out of place.
You remember some of the others because Sidney had trouble remembering when we interviewed him.
Louis Cottrell was on clarinet and sax. Joe Phillips, another trumpet player. You had Louren Nelson on trombone.
He's one of the few he could remember.
Yeah, and you had Kimball, who was playing guitar. He's now playing bass. Yeah.
And oh I- Henry Kimball, the old man who played bass too. No, not him, I'm talking about- It was his son, was it?

Yeah. Mrs. Kimball was a piano player, her husband. With Celestan. Yeah. He used to play with Celestan too, but at that time he was playing with Sidney. And they had a wonderful band. And I'm telling you the truth Bill, those people really, they learned me something. Because when I got with that band, I could play the chords, but Sidney had a lot of stock arrangement, they didn't write chords out too much. And man they used to cut me every night. I was working 24 hours a day with the band because I had to take two, three numbers home every night and practice all day until I finally made it with the band. And I become one of the best piano players that he had because I played the way he wanted. And I played the rhythm and just in orchestration a little part would come in for the piano and I'd study that and I'd be able to make it. I remember an experience I had one time that Morton and Moulin came down with an old 16 piece band and they didn't have any piano player. And the leader of the band at that time, I forget his name, Ag Sidney could have used me. And man I told him, I said listen man, Sidney's band was bad enough, I mean the music they had. And these guys was playing strictly arrangements you know, they were really more modern than Sidney's band. And I told him man I couldn't make it. So he said oh come on and try you know. So fortunately when I got up there all the music was written in chords you know. And when they ever had a solo for the piano they just had a solo and you had to break the chord.
And that was right up my alley man.

So we were getting I think $13, Sidney had two bands. Sidney got $13, they played before the other band. And this band was getting $20. So I worked both bands that night and I played so well with this band because they were fellows were getting off you know, there was modern saxophone playing trumpets getting off. And all they wanted was somebody to chord. Well I had got my experience from this first place job I worked at the Pelican by letting these fellows jam and chord with them. See and they loved the way I played. And he offered to give me $25 a night for 32 dates. They were going up to New York and I got cold feet and I wouldn't take it. I had heard so much about these New York musicians I was afraid to go you know. So I worked all around Bourbon until George went to New York with Bump. And I know you remember I went to New York with them.

And you stayed with George. Yeah I stayed with George. In California. I was going to ask you in particular about some more of the piano players, a lot of the guys I wouldn't know like you didn't because I wasn't there. But Steve Lewis, I know one time some friend of mine talked to you about Steve Lewis. Can you tell us something about him?

Well I was pretty young and I didn't know too much about Steve outside he was a good piano player. And he could sing all kind of risky numbers and different things like that. And he played with P-Rone's band. But I didn't know too much about Steve. I saw him a couple of times. Because they had a contest on the Estora for the best piano player and my little friend that taught me, started me off playing, Bourbon, won the contest from Steve Lewis and Walter Pichon, who were the top piano players in New Orleans at the time. I know. But this guy was so fast he was a great piano man.
Bruno couldn't read.

He couldn't read a note as big as a boxcar. No. But man, he played anything he'd hear. Anything. Don't care what it was. He played. And that's where I saw Steve. I had the, when I was little we had, I used to live around where they had these what you would call hunky-tongs. And they had the one on Orleans near Liberty that they called the Blues Breakers. And I had the pleasure of listening to a fellow by the name of Udell playing. Who used to make, I don't know, I just know about Udell. He made piano rolls. The best talks about it.
Yeah.
Well I, now remember I couldn't go in the ballrooms at this time.
You say he made piano rolls? Yeah. I didn't know that.

Yeah. That's what they told me, that he used to make piano rolls. And we used to sit on the crib and the sidewalk and look in the ballroom, you know, they had these little doors that cut from the top and bottom. And I used to listen to these piano players. Then they had a place on the wagon top where they had a wonderful Boogie Woogie piano player. We used to call him Boogie Woogie. He was a cripple fellow. And he used to play some, but that's before Boogie Woogie, I never heard any other thing about Boogie Woogie then, yeah. And I'll tell you an experience, you know, they had a lot of piano players. Everybody could play staggley or how long on the piano. And when I was learning they had a piano player by the name of Papa Crutch, he wasn't very good. Papa Crutch they used to call him. Yeah, he'd beat on the piano with his hand and everything. He was a real showman, you know. And a lot of times in these ballrooms when I would practice and he'd come in there and he'd say, get up boy, get off that piano, you don't know what you're doing. And I'd get so angry at him and I'd promise myself that someday I'd run him off a piano. And I didn't get that opportunity. You know I used to buck in New Orleans, everywhere there was musicians there would buck, you know. So you would either have to play or you'd better stay inside.
Where was it that you finally evened up the sky?

In one of the ballrooms I walked in and he was sitting down playing you know. I'd say get up man, you don't know how to play. He was so surprised. Also I had another fellow who taught me a lot on the piano. He was a very good musician but he played nice. His name was Plutsem. Plutsem? Yeah. His last name was Johnson. But we used to call him Plutsem. He was hunchback. And he taught me a whole lot on piano. Well I wish I would continue learning because now that I'm playing I'm a little handicapped in some of the things I really would like to do. I knew it but I started off with the wrong fingering of piano. And now I've got to practice and practice and practice to break the habit of playing one certain way you know.
When you were a kid did you ever have a piano in your home to practice?
I never did have a piano in my home.
I guess you began working professionally before you owned the piano. Oh yeah.

To tell the truth Bill I guess I was playing real long until I would say 12-14 years ago that I got a piano of my own. I played all the time. When I went to practice I'd go to a ball. They had pianos in all the balls then you know. And I would practice there. I never did have a piano.

What about the dance halls? Some of those real old time bands you know didn't even use the piano they say. Were there some of the dance halls like economy or hope solar cooperating? Did they all have pianos in them?

They had pianos in them but they had very few piano players you know that played with bands. They used to use banjo because I used to hear them and they used to before a band would go in the hall and play they used to play outside you know. And they used to use the banjos. And then whenever a band could get a good piano player why they would get it. But these jazz bands are you know, most of the good piano players were working with bands like P. Rowan, Celestan, who used to get the best jobs. And they were working singles too playing in Storyville. And when I say Storyville I don't remember when Storyville was really open but when they were open illegal I remember that. You know I used to go there.
After you were seven years old they were supposed to be closed but they kept running the houses.

Yeah, houses were still operating and Bourbon Street wasn't open then. They didn't have nothing like Bourbon Street see. And illegally these houses used to run and different piano players would play in them. Because I played some job myself.
Did they have any bands up in the district there say along the Basin or Ivoryville? Yeah, they had bands.
I'm a favorite.
Well this place I heard some guys talking about San Francisco might have been orion but you've been talking about the alley. Is that the Eclipse alley that George named the band?

No, no. The alley was on St. Bernard and Claiborne. Right behind, that's where the Seminard Market was. And in the back of the Seminard Market they had allies leading from Seminard off to Claiborne. And right in the back there they had a cabaret.
That's what they called the alley.
That's what they called the alley, yeah.
Oh I didn't know.
That wasn't in Sturryville at all.
No, oh no. No.
That's why I heard Guy Kelly there. Guy Kelly.

Who was the, I guess you sort of picked your pianist saying Vernell, San Diego was the best and greatest you ever heard. Would you say that or who would be your favorite? Well. Of the New Orleans pianos.

I wouldn't have to say Vernell was my favorite piano player, although he couldn't read. But there was nothing that he heard that he couldn't play. I mean when Earl Hines was popular, he would, when he'd sit down at the piano he liked the kid, he would listen on it and he was a lot of fun. And he would listen at a record and he'd play like that record. Then he would play, then he'd say this is the way I would play it. And he'd play the way he would play it and it would get better and better all the time. So if he was a boy, well I guess if he knew music he wouldn't have had the ideas he had. But Pichon, his ideas were the greatest ideas I ever heard. Pichon wanted to teach him music if he would just show him some of the ideas that he had. See Pichon is a great writer of music. And boy he didn't want to learn how to read music or nothing like that. But I would have to say he's the best, although I mean he didn't play like the music would go, you know, but man he could play piano with his toes.
You mean he really did?

I'm not, I'm proud of, he'd take the back of his hand and play piano like that. I'd run with him all of his time. Him and I was just like brothers. Was he much older than you or any older? I was older than him.
Was that older than him?

Yeah, I was older than him. He was a young guy and a very good looking guy. He looked like something like an Indian. He had cold black hair. And he, man he had the fastest fingers. He played any kind of music.
He died when he was quite young. Yeah.

I worked in intermission. I was playing intermission for him at Gaspar's on Bourbon Street. And they had an opera at one of the places in New Orleans. And the conductor came after. And Gaspar knew Bourbon, the man who owned the place was Gaspar. He knew Bourbon could play. And he came up and told Bourbon, he said, here's a long-haired guy. And he said, I want you to play something for him. And Bourbon played a classic that the man jumped up and said it can't be done. Honest. He said it just can't be done. A man just can't play that good.
That's how great he was. That's right.
And so many people came band, Duke Ellington's band and them used to come through and hear him playing want to take him just as a soloist, but he never would leave. He was, man he was a genius.
Yeah. Never made a record or anything?

Never made none, no records or nothing. It's really pitiful. Of course Bourbon was gifted, his whole family played. Just one of the brothers, he had about seven in the family and just one brother couldn't play. But all these little sisters and everything, the mother. Willie San Diego, the great banjo player was his uncle I think. He was that musical family. Yeah. But Bourbon could play before his feet could touch the ground. Yeah.
You know. Well we're getting near the end of this. Is there anything else you'd like to add on here? Well. Well. Well. I.

I just like to add that I like the jazz. When I went to New York with Bunk's band, Bill, I could have made more money playing with Smiling Joe. But I like the jazz so much that I'd rather be with them. And right now, Bill, I think that George Lewis who has the band, has one of the greatest authentic jazz bands that ever live in. And that there will never be another band like his after those minutes have passed. Well they got on record a lot of times. A lot of people have heard you all over the world.
Yeah. So that last part of his career, so the last few years is well recorded there too. Yeah, I made a lot of recording with them and I sure miss them, Bill.
And I wish that someday that I could get that band back together. Yeah. And I really would like to get them back.
I think I just about all want to thank you for the interview and best of luck to you.
Yeah, Bill. Thank you. Thank you.

segments.title: Birth in the old Quarter, parents and brother
segments.summary: Purnell gives his birth date and address, his father's drumming, his saxophonist brother, and the move to a Black neighborhood around age nine or ten.

segments.title: First music: tailgate wagons, bread-box drumming, Cooperators Hall bands
segments.summary: He first heard advertising-truck jazz and drummed on bread boxes; living by Cooperators Hall he heard the great bands and sneaked out to listen.

segments.title: Church singing and learning piano chords from a friend
segments.summary: Church on Liberty and St. Peter, preachers and choirs, singing at school and house parties; a young piano friend showed him chords and Indian Love Call.

segments.title: Brother's rehearsals and his first paid job
segments.summary: His brother's band rehearsed at home; Purnell got his first job as a singer and two-piece pianist during the depression and was paid fifteen dollars.

segments.title: Cheap jobs, the Pelican job and Walter Pichon's lessons
segments.summary: He played cheap jobs, took a banjoist's offered job at the Pelican where steamer musicians jammed, and learned music from Walter Pichon.

segments.title: Isaiah Morgan's band, then Bourbon Street jobs with George Lewis and Smilin' Joe
segments.summary: Isaiah took over Sam Morgan's band and Purnell toured two or three years; afterwards he worked early Bourbon Street trios, an army camp job with George Lewis, and the Famous Door.

segments.title: Getting the piano chair in Sidney Desvigne's band
segments.summary: Desvigne's piano player went on vacation and Purnell filled in among better pianists; Sidney was strict about playing his music as written.

segments.title: Desvigne band personnel and learning the stock arrangements
segments.summary: He names the band members and describes practising numbers all day to learn the stock arrangements.

segments.title: Sitting in with a modern 16-piece band and the New York offer
segments.summary: A visiting arranged band needed a chord pianist; he excelled, was offered $25 a night to go to New York but declined from nerves.

segments.title: Steve Lewis and the piano contest won by his friend
segments.summary: Asked about Steve Lewis, he recalls the boat contest won by his non-reading friend, and hearing Udell in honky-tonks.

segments.title: Listening at ballrooms; Papa Crutch and Plutsem
segments.summary: He listened at ballroom doors, heard a boogie woogie player, was chased off pianos by Papa Crutch, and learned from the hunchback Plutsem.

segments.title: Never owning a piano; practising in ballrooms
segments.summary: He had no piano at home until twelve to fourteen years ago, practising in ballrooms instead.

segments.title: Pianos in dance halls, banjos, and illegal Storyville houses
segments.summary: Old halls had pianos but bands often used banjo; good pianists worked with top bands or in Storyville houses, which ran illegally after closing.

segments.title: The Alley cabaret behind Seminard Market
segments.summary: Purnell clarifies the Alley was at St. Bernard and Claiborne behind the market, not in Storyville, where he heard Guy Kelly.

segments.title: Choosing his favorite pianist: his friend's genius
segments.summary: He names his non-reading friend the best, able to copy any record and improve on it, with Pichon's ideas also admired.

segments.title: Gaspar's, the opera conductor, and his unrecorded family of musicians
segments.summary: Playing intermission at Gaspar's, he saw the friend astonish an opera conductor; he never recorded, from a musical family.

segments.title: Closing thoughts on Bunk's band and George Lewis
segments.summary: He prefers jazz to better money, praises George Lewis's band as authentic, and wishes to reunite it.

segments.title: Thanks and goodbye
segments.summary: Russell thanks Purnell and the interview ends.
